Circuit Court of Appeals, sitting en banc, ruled in June 2001 in a unanimous per curiam opinion that largely upheld the core liability — Microsoft had illegally maintained its monopoly through exclusionary conduct — but reversed the tying claim for retrial under a different standard, and vacated the breakup entirely. Critically, the court removed Judge Jackson from the case for serious judicial misconduct: he had given secret interviews to reporters during the trial, comparing Microsoft executives to gangland killers and Gates to Napoleon. The remedy was remanded to a new judge, Colleen Kollar-Kotelly, and the new Bush administration's Justice Department announced it would no longer seek breakup. A settlement was reached in November 2001 and approved in 2002: Microsoft agreed to share APIs with third parties, license protocols, refrain from retaliating against PC makers who shipped rival software, and accept a technical oversight committee — but it kept IE in Windows and kept the company whole. Nine states dissented as the terms being too weak; the consent decree ultimately ran until 2011. Europe pressed harder: the European Commission fined Microsoft 497 million euros in 2004 over media-player bundling and server interoperability, added further fines for non-compliance reaching 899 million euros (reduced on appeal to 860 million), and a 2009 settlement forced a browser-choice ballot screen into European Windows.

The trial's legacy is debated but real. Formally Microsoft escaped nearly intact; behaviorally, insiders and observers — including Gates himself in later interviews — described a company made cautious, lawyered and distracted just as the internet's next platforms emerged. Microsoft would spend the 2000s watching Google conquer search and advertising and Apple conquer music and mobile, constrained less by the consent decree's text than by the institutional scar tissue it left. The case also became the template for platform-antitrust thinking that regulators would apply, two decades later, to Google, Apple, Amazon and Meta.

sections.heading: Windows XP, the Enterprise Machine and the Security Reckoning (2000–2006)
sections.body:
Steve Ballmer became chief executive in January 2000, with Gates stepping back to a new role as chairman and chief software architect, and the company's flagship achievement of the era arrived on October 25, 2001: Windows XP. XP finally unified the two Windows bloodlines, putting the NT kernel's stability under a consumer-friendly shell for everyone, and it landed. Businesses that had suffered Windows 98's crashes and skipped Windows Me standardized on XP for over a decade; it became, by most measures, the most widely deployed operating system in history to that point, with an installed base eventually exceeding a billion machines when counting its long afterlife. That afterlife was itself extraordinary: mainstream support ran to 2009, extended support to April 2014, and XP still ran ATMs, retail terminals and industrial systems years after that — a longevity that testified both to the product's adequacy and to how badly its successor stumbled.

The same years forced a security reckoning. The internet-connected Windows monoculture proved a paradise for worms: Code Red and Nimda in 2001, SQL Slammer — which doubled its infections every 8.5 seconds and disrupted networks worldwide in minutes — and Blaster in 2003, Sasser in 2004. The reputational damage was severe enough that in January 2002 Gates issued his Trustworthy Computing memo to every employee, declaring that security must now trump features. Development on new features effectively paused while thousands of engineers underwent secure-coding training and audited old code; the Security Development Lifecycle became mandatory process; and Windows XP Service Pack 2 in 2004 — a free release so substantial it functioned as a new operating system — turned on the firewall by default, added memory protections and rebuilt the update pipeline into the automatic Windows Update regime that persists today. The episode is still taught as a case study in a giant company turning its engineering culture in mid-flight.

Meanwhile the quieter half of Microsoft compounded: the enterprise. Windows Server (2000, 2003) with Active Directory became the default directory and identity system of corporate computing, displacing Novell; Exchange became the world's mail server; SQL Server grew from a mid-market database into a genuine Oracle competitor; SharePoint spread through intranets; and Visual Studio plus the .NET Framework, launched in 2002 with the C# language designed by Anders Hejlsberg (recruited from Borland, where he had created Delphi), rebuilt Microsoft's developer franchise for the web era. Software Assurance and enterprise agreements converted corporate customers into predictable annuity revenue. This business — unsexy, sticky and vastly profitable — is what funded the 2000s' consumer misadventures and later became the launchpad for Azure: the salesforce, the account relationships and the identity plumbing were already inside every large organization on earth.

The era's ledger also carries its warnings. Microsoft's stock went essentially sideways for the entire decade despite revenue tripling — the market had priced in perfection in 1999 and spent ten years digesting it. Longhorn, the ambitious successor to XP announced in 2003 with database-backed file storage (WinFS), a new graphics layer and managed-code foundations, collapsed under its own weight and had to be reset in 2004, its remnants shipping in 2007 as Windows Vista: late, hardware-hungry, nagging users with security prompts, and received as the company's most public failure in years. Vista's flop, XP's stubborn persistence, Google's IPO in 2004, and Apple's iPod ascendancy framed the question that would dominate the next chapter: had Microsoft become a company that could execute everywhere except the future?

sections.heading: The Ballmer Paradox: Record Profits and Missed Waves (2006–2013)
sections.body:
The Ballmer years present a genuine paradox that honest history has to hold in both hands. Financially, the record is strong: revenue grew from about 23 billion dollars in fiscal 2000 to nearly 78 billion in fiscal 2013, profits roughly tripled, and the enterprise, Office and server businesses executed superbly. Strategically, the same years contain the most consequential misses in the company's history, and the stock's decade of stagnation reflects which story investors believed.

The defining miss was mobile. Microsoft was early — Windows Mobile and Pocket PC devices predated the iPhone by years — but its model of licensing a stylus-driven, desktop-like OS to hardware partners was annihilated by Apple's January 2007 iPhone. Ballmer's contemporaneous reaction became the era's epitaph: he laughed that the iPhone had no chance of getting significant market share at a 500-dollar subsidized price. Google then gave Android away free, inverting Microsoft's own licensing playbook. Microsoft's rebuilt answer, Windows Phone 7 (2010) and the elegant tile-based Windows Phone 8, earned critical praise and commercial irrelevance — trapped in the app-ecosystem chicken-and-egg it had once inflicted on OS/2. The February 2011 partnership that made Nokia, the world's largest phone maker, exclusive to Windows Phone ended with Microsoft buying Nokia's devices business in September 2013 for about 7.2 billion dollars — a deal Ballmer pushed over significant board resistance in his final months — and writing off substantially all of it (7.6 billion dollars) in 2015, exiting phones entirely.

Search and advertising was the other great miss. Google's rise on the back of search ads happened in plain sight; Microsoft's responses — MSN Search, Live Search, and in 2009 the genuinely well-built Bing — never dented Google's share materially, and the 2008 attempt to buy Yahoo for about 44.6 billion dollars, rebuffed by Yahoo's board, looks in retrospect like a bullet dodged. Online services lost billions across the decade. Other stumbles were smaller but telling: the Zune music player (2006) arrived five years after the iPod; the Kin phones (2010) were killed within weeks; Windows 8 (2012), a bold attempt to force a touch-tablet interface onto a mouse-and-keyboard world, alienated the core user base badly enough that Windows 8.1 hurriedly restored the Start button, and Windows 10 (2015) was pitched explicitly as a return to familiarity.

Yet the same regime planted much of what later flourished. Ballmer green-lit Azure (announced 2008, launched 2010 under Ray Ozzie's cloud push) and hired Satya Nadella to run the server-and-tools business that housed it. Office 365 began the subscription transition in 2011. Kinect (2010) became the fastest-selling consumer electronics device on record, moving eight million units in sixty days. SharePoint, Dynamics, System Center and SQL Server compounded quietly. The acquisition record was mixed on both sides of the ledger: aQuantive (6.3 billion dollars, 2007) was written off almost entirely, and Skype (8.5 billion, 2011) was ultimately eclipsed by Teams and finally shut down in 2025 — but Skype's infrastructure and consumer reach mattered in the meantime, and the 2012 purchase of Yammer signaled the social-enterprise turn. Ballmer announced his retirement in August 2013; the stock rose on the news, a cruel verdict on a tenure that had, in fact, built a great deal of the foundation his successor would monetize. The fair summary may be that Ballmer's Microsoft won every war it chose to fight with its existing weapons and lost every war that required new ones — and that the distinction between those two categories is the entire art of running a technology company.

sections.heading: Xbox and Gaming: From Console Newcomer to the Activision Blizzard Megadeal
sections.body:
Microsoft entered the console business as a defensive move that became a durable third pillar. In the late 1990s, Sony was openly positioning the PlayStation 2 as the entertainment hub of the living room — a computing beachhead that Redmond feared could grow into a rival platform. A skunkworks team including Seamus Blackley, Kevin Bachus, Ted Hase and Otto Berkes pitched a DirectX box — essentially a PC-derived console built around Microsoft's DirectX graphics APIs — and Gates approved it. The original Xbox launched on November 15, 2001 at 299 dollars, a muscular machine with a built-in hard drive and Ethernet port, both console firsts. It lost money on every unit — the gaming division's losses across the first console generation ran into the billions — but it established two franchise assets: Halo: Combat Evolved, the launch title from newly acquired Bungie that defined console shooters, and Xbox Live (2002), the subscription online service whose friends lists, voice chat and matchmaking became the template the whole industry copied. The Xbox sold roughly 24 million units against the PlayStation 2's 155-plus million, but it bought Microsoft a seat at the table.

The Xbox 360, launched in November 2005 a full year ahead of the PlayStation 3, was the high point of Microsoft's console competitiveness. Its head start, superior online service, and franchises like Halo 3 and Gears of War made it the preferred platform of the HD generation in North America; it ultimately sold about 84 million units, essentially tied with the PS3 worldwide. The triumph carried an expensive scar: the Red Ring of Death, a systemic hardware failure from thermal design flaws, forced a 2007 warranty extension that cost more than a billion dollars — accepted by leadership as the price of keeping customer trust. Kinect, the 2010 motion-sensing camera, added a genuine phenomenon, selling eight million units in sixty days as the fastest-selling consumer device on record.

The Xbox One's November 2013 launch squandered nearly all of it. Priced 100 dollars above the PlayStation 4 because of a bundled Kinect few wanted, initially announced with always-online requirements and used-game restrictions that had to be reversed amid consumer revolt, and pitched as a TV-centric entertainment box rather than a games machine, it was decisively outsold — estimates put it around 58 million units against the PS4's 117 million. Phil Spencer, made head of Xbox in 2014, spent the generation rebuilding: buying Mojang and Minecraft for 2.5 billion dollars in 2014 (Minecraft, the best-selling game of all time at over 300 million copies, was left multiplatform — a signal of the new strategy), assembling studios like Obsidian, inXile and Double Fine, and launching Xbox Game Pass in 2017, a Netflix-style subscription that redefined the business model around access rather than unit sales.

The strategy culminated in acquisitions of historic scale: ZeniMax Media, parent of Bethesda (Doom, Fallout, The Elder Scrolls), for 7.5 billion dollars, closing 2021; then Activision Blizzard — Call of Duty, World of Warcraft, Candy Crush — announced January 2022 at 68.7 billion dollars, the largest acquisition in gaming history and in Microsoft's history. Regulators put the deal through twenty-one months of scrutiny: the U.S. FTC sued to block it and lost in federal court, and the UK's Competition and Markets Authority forced a restructuring in which cloud-streaming rights for Activision titles went to Ubisoft before clearing the deal on October 13, 2023. The combined company became roughly the world's third-largest gaming business by revenue behind Tencent and Sony — an industry, it is worth remembering, now larger than global film and music combined — with the Series X/S consoles (2020), Game Pass, cloud streaming and a multiplatform publishing posture (including, by 2024–25, shipping former exclusives on PlayStation) defining a strategy in which the console is one endpoint among many rather than the product itself.

sections.heading: Satya Nadella, Cloud First and the Azure Turnaround (2014 Onward)
sections.body:
On February 4, 2014, Satya Nadella became Microsoft's third chief executive — a 22-year company veteran, born in Hyderabad in 1967, who had run the server and tools division and then the fledgling cloud business. The same announcement ended an era: Gates left the chairmanship (he would leave the board entirely in 2020), and John Thompson became chairman. Nadella's changes were first cultural and rhetorical, and mocked by cynics as soft until the numbers made them unanswerable. He reframed the company's mission — to empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more — replaced the internal stack-ranking review system that had institutionalized knife-fighting between teams, preached learn-it-all over know-it-all (borrowing Carol Dweck's growth-mindset language), and, most substantively, ended the strategy of using Windows as the gravitational center to which everything else must be tethered.

The symbols came fast and deliberately. Within two months, Office arrived on Apple's iPad — a product held hostage for years under the old logic that it must favor Windows tablets. Microsoft joined the Linux Foundation and declared, through Azure executive Mark Russinovich and then Nadella himself, that Microsoft loves Linux — a sentence unimaginable from the company whose former CEO had called Linux a cancer in 2001. .NET was open-sourced; the Windows Subsystem for Linux put a genuine Linux environment inside Windows; Visual Studio Code, released free and open-source in 2015, became the world's most popular code editor; and the 2018 GitHub acquisition (7.5 billion dollars in stock) placed Microsoft as steward of open source's home. Each move traded a little Windows leverage for a claim on developers wherever they were — the exact inversion of the 1990s playbook.

The economic engine of the turnaround was Azure. Launched in 2010 as Windows Azure and renamed Microsoft Azure in 2014, it ran a distant second to Amazon Web Services, which had invented the cloud-infrastructure market in 2006. Nadella's Microsoft poured capital into data centers — spending that reached tens of billions of dollars a year — and leveraged its unmatched enterprise distribution: the identity system (Active Directory extended into Azure AD, later Entra), the account relationships, hybrid-cloud tooling for companies unwilling to abandon their server rooms, and enterprise agreements that made Azure the path of least resistance for Windows-and-Office shops. Commercial cloud revenue — Azure plus Office 365, Dynamics and LinkedIn's commercial pieces — passed an annualized run rate of 100 billion dollars by the mid-2020s, with Azure holding a solid second place around a quarter of the global infrastructure market. Office 365's subscription conversion completed under the Microsoft 365 brand; LinkedIn, acquired in 2016 for 26.2 billion dollars — then Microsoft's largest deal — grew past 15 billion dollars in annual revenue; Teams rode the pandemic to hundreds of millions of users; Surface hardware, begun awkwardly in 2012 with a near-billion-dollar RT write-off, matured into a respectable premium line.

The market's verdict was emphatic. Microsoft's stock, which had ended the Ballmer era roughly where it began, multiplied more than tenfold under Nadella's first decade. The company passed one trillion dollars of market value in April 2019, two trillion in June 2021, and in January 2024 became the second company ever to cross three trillion, trading places with Apple for the title of world's most valuable. Behind the numbers lay a strategic identity that finally cohered: Microsoft as the neutral, trusted utility of business computing — selling the picks and shovels of the digital economy to every side, on every platform, exactly as it had once sold BASIC to every microcomputer maker. The stage was set for the company to make the largest bet of its modern era, on artificial intelligence.

sections.heading: The OpenAI Partnership and the AI Era
sections.body:
Microsoft's dominant position in the AI era was purchased with an early, unfashionable bet. In July 2019 the company invested one billion dollars in OpenAI, the San Francisco research lab founded in 2015 by Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Ilya Sutskever, Greg Brockman and others, which had restructured into a capped-profit company to fund the enormous computing costs of training large models. The deal made Azure OpenAI's exclusive cloud provider — Microsoft built dedicated supercomputing clusters, stuffed with tens of thousands of NVIDIA GPUs, ranked among the world's most powerful — and gave Microsoft a license to commercialize OpenAI's technology. A second investment followed in 2021, and in January 2023, weeks after ChatGPT's explosive debut on November 30, 2022 (a hundred million users within two months, the fastest-growing consumer application in history to that point), Microsoft committed a further tranche widely reported at ten billion dollars, structured to return the bulk of OpenAI's profits to Microsoft until thresholds were met, alongside a stake commonly described as around 49 percent of the capped-profit entity's equity interests.

The first mass-market fruit was GitHub Copilot, launched generally in 2022: an AI pair-programmer built on OpenAI's Codex that autocompleted whole functions, and the proof that generative models could be productized as assistants inside existing tools. In February 2023 Nadella brought the fight directly to Google, relaunching Bing with a GPT-4-powered chat mode and telling reporters, memorably, that he wanted to make Google dance. Bing's search share barely moved — Google's distribution proved as durable as Microsoft's once had — but the copilot pattern spread through the entire product line: Microsoft 365 Copilot (drafting documents, summarizing meetings, building spreadsheets) at 30 dollars per user per month for enterprises, Copilots in Dynamics, in security tools, in Windows itself, and Azure OpenAI Service selling raw model access to corporations. The company that missed mobile had positioned itself, through one partnership, at the front of the next platform shift; NVIDIA aside, no incumbent captured more of the generative-AI moment.

The partnership survived a stress test that briefly threatened everything. On November 17, 2023, OpenAI's nonprofit board abruptly fired Sam Altman without warning Microsoft. Nadella responded within days by announcing that Altman, Brockman and any departing OpenAI staff would join a new Microsoft AI lab — a maneuver that, with an open revolt by more than 700 of OpenAI's roughly 770 employees, forced Altman's reinstatement inside a week. Microsoft took a non-voting board observer seat (later relinquished as regulators in the EU, UK and US began examining whether the partnership amounted to an unreviewed merger). Microsoft simultaneously hedged: it hired Mustafa Suleyman, the DeepMind and Inflection AI co-founder, in March 2024 to run a new consumer Microsoft AI division — absorbing most of Inflection's team in a 650-million-dollar licensing arrangement that itself drew antitrust attention — invested in and hosted rival models (Meta's Llama, Mistral, xAI's Grok on Azure), and built its own in-house model family. In 2025 the partnership was restructured again as OpenAI converted its for-profit arm to a public benefit corporation, with Microsoft's stake valued in the hundreds of billions and the exclusivity terms loosened in both directions.

The AI buildout reshaped the company's physical and financial profile: capital expenditures soared past 50 and then toward 80-plus billion dollars a year for data centers, power contracts (including a deal to restart a reactor at Three Mile Island), and custom silicon (the Maia AI accelerator and Cobalt CPU, announced 2023). It also revived old questions in new form — copyright suits from the New York Times and authors over training data, scrutiny of AI's energy demands, and the recurring regulatory suspicion that attends any company standing at a platform choke point. Fifty years after two teenagers licensed a BASIC interpreter for a kit computer, the wager was structurally identical: supply the essential software layer for a new kind of machine, and charge everyone.

sections.heading: Acquisitions, Culture and Leadership: How the Company Actually Changed Hands and Habits
sections.body:
Microsoft's trajectory is inseparable from a handful of leadership transitions and a long, instructive acquisition record. The company has had only three chief executives in half a century: Gates (1975–2000), Ballmer (2000–2014) and Nadella (2014–). Gates's transitions were deliberately staged — CEO to chief software architect in 2000, day-to-day departure in 2008 to focus on the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, board exit in 2020 — and his shadow shaped the institution long after his badge access mattered: the memo culture (the Internet Tidal Wave in 1995, Trustworthy Computing in 2002), the think-week ritual, and the assumption that the CEO must be able to argue technology with engineers. Paul Allen's story ran differently: gone from operations in 1983 after his cancer diagnosis and never returning, he chronicled his estrangement from Gates — including overhearing Gates and Ballmer discussing diluting his stake — in his 2011 memoir Idea Man, spent his fortune on the Seattle Seahawks, Portland Trail Blazers, brain-science research and rock-and-roll museums, and died of non-Hodgkin lymphoma complications in October 2018, with Gates at his bedside in their final months of reconciliation.

The acquisition ledger, more than 250 deals, teaches by contrast. The disasters cluster where Microsoft bought its way into markets it did not understand or bought to deny others: aQuantive (6.3 billion dollars, 2007) written off almost entirely within five years; Nokia's phones (7.2 billion, 2014) written off the following year with 7,800 layoffs; Danger, whose Sidekick data loss became a cloud-era cautionary tale. The triumphs cluster where Microsoft bought communities and let them alone: Minecraft (2.5 billion, 2014) kept multiplatform and grew into the best-selling game ever; LinkedIn (26.2 billion, 2016) retained its brand and leadership and tripled its revenue; GitHub (7.5 billion, 2018) kept its CEO, its culture and its neutrality, growing from 28 million to over 100 million developers while incubating Copilot. Skype (8.5 billion, 2011) sits in the middle: strategically useful, ultimately cannibalized by Teams and retired in 2025. The lesson Nadella's team drew explicitly — buy the network, protect its independence, monetize through the cloud — guided the ZeniMax and Activision Blizzard deals, where studio autonomy was a stated principle even as 68.7 billion dollars changed hands.

Culture is the thread that connects the eras. The Gates-era company was brilliant, combative and paranoid — develop for the platform, crush the adjacent, document everything in email (a habit the antitrust trial punished). The Ballmer era added scale and sales discipline but curdled internally: the stack-ranking performance system, which forced every team to grade a fixed share of its members as failures, was blamed by a famous 2012 Vanity Fair investigation, Microsoft's Lost Decade, for a decade of infighting in which employees competed against each other rather than competitors. Ballmer abolished stack ranking in 2013; Nadella built its replacement around growth mindset, customer obsession and the once-heretical idea that Microsoft wins by making others productive on any platform. Skeptics note, fairly, that the kinder vocabulary coincided with ruthless commercial aggression — Teams bundling, aggressive enterprise licensing, and layoffs exceeding 10,000 in 2023 and continuing in the AI-spending years even amid record profits.

Gates's personal standing also shifted: his 2021 divorce from Melinda French Gates after 27 years, reporting on his conduct with employees and his contacts with Jeffrey Epstein, and his board departure complicated the elder-statesman image, even as the Gates Foundation — endowed with the bulk of his and Warren Buffett's fortunes — became the largest private philanthropy in history, credited with a central role in global vaccination campaigns. The company he left behind had, by its fiftieth anniversary in April 2025, some 228,000 employees and revenue above 245 billion dollars a year — run by an Indian-born engineer, its code on GitHub, its profits from renting Linux servers as happily as Windows ones, an outcome no observer of 1995 would have wagered on.

sections.heading: Legacy and Criticism: What Microsoft Changed and What It Costs
sections.body:
Any honest accounting of Microsoft's first half-century has to run two columns simultaneously, because the same facts appear in both. Start with the transformative column. Microsoft, more than any single company, made the computer a commodity: by decoupling software from hardware and licensing MS-DOS and Windows to all comers, it created the brutal clone competition that drove PC prices down relentlessly and put more than a billion machines into homes, schools and businesses within three decades of the IBM PC. It standardized the world's office work — Word documents, Excel spreadsheets and PowerPoint decks are the lingua franca of modern administration, for better and demonstrably sometimes for worse — and its developer tools, from QuickBASIC through Visual Basic to Visual Studio, C#, TypeScript (Anders Hejlsberg's 2012 language that now underpins much of the web) and VS Code, lowered the barriers to programming for tens of millions. Xbox Live wrote the grammar of online console play; Azure's data centers run a substantial fraction of the world's institutions; and the Kinect-to-HoloLens-to-Copilot line shows a company that never stopped shipping research into products, even when the products failed.

The critical column is just as factual. The methods that built the empire — bundling, exclusive OEM contracts, embrace-extend-extinguish (a phrase from Microsoft's own internal documents describing its approach to internet standards), leveraging one monopoly to seed the next — were found unlawful by U.S. courts and fined repeatedly by the European Commission, and they demonstrably narrowed consumer choice for years: the IE 6 stagnation, when Microsoft won the browser war and then stopped improving the browser for half a decade, is the canonical case of monopoly's cost appearing not as high prices but as absent innovation. The Windows security monoculture imposed enormous externalized costs in the worm era. Competitors from Digital Research and Netscape to WordPerfect, Lotus, Borland and Novell furnish a graveyard tour of the platform owner's advantages. And the modern company attracts modern versions of the old complaints: Teams bundled into Microsoft 365 (drawing an EU statement of objections in 2024, echoing 2004's media-player case), aggressive cloud licensing terms under regulatory review in Europe and the UK, the 2024 CrowdStrike incident and repeated nation-state breaches of its cloud renewing questions about concentration risk, and its OpenAI entanglement examined by antitrust agencies on three continents.

The historiographic point is that both columns describe one mechanism. Microsoft's genius, from Altair BASIC to Copilot, has been to identify the choke point of each computing era — the language runtime, the operating system, the office suite, the enterprise directory, the cloud, the model layer — occupy it early or buy into it, and monetize it across everyone else's hardware and everyone else's applications. Choke points create standards, and standards create both the enormous consumer surplus of compatibility and the enormous private power that regulators exist to check. The company's own history demonstrates the check working imperfectly but not negligibly: the antitrust years plausibly cost Microsoft the mobile era and thereby created the room in which Google and Apple built the smartphone world.

For a reader in the AI era, the history reads less like a museum piece than a forecast. A fifty-year-old company sits again at a possible choke point — compute, models and the assistant layer — with governments again circling, partners again wary, and the founding wager again in play: that whoever supplies the indispensable software layer of the new machines will, for a generation, quietly tax the future. Whether the third act ends like the desktop era, the mobile era, or somewhere new is the live question; the pattern, at least, is now well documented.

guides.title: History of IBM
guides.summary: The story of IBM from Herman Hollerith's census tabulators and the 1911 CTR merger through the punched-card era, the System/360 gamble, the PC and the clone wars, the 1990s crisis and services turnaround, to Deep Blue, Watson, Red Hat, and quantum computing.

sections.heading: Herman Hollerith and the 1890 Census
sections.body:
IBM's deepest root is a data-processing crisis in the United States government. The Constitution requires a census every ten years, and by the late nineteenth century the country was growing faster than clerks could count it. The 1880 census, tallied entirely by hand, took the better part of eight years to process, and officials projected that the 1890 count might not be finished before the 1900 census began. Herman Hollerith, born in Buffalo, New York, in 1860 to German immigrant parents, was a young engineer trained at Columbia's School of Mines who briefly worked for the Census Office. There the physician and statistician John Shaw Billings remarked to him that the tallying ought to be done by machine, perhaps with cards on the model of the Jacquard loom, which had controlled weaving patterns with punched cards since the early 1800s. Railroad conductors punching descriptions into tickets supplied another spark. Hollerith spent the 1880s turning the idea into hardware and filed his foundational patents in 1884 and 1889.

His system had three parts that would define data processing for the next seventy years. A punch clerk recorded each person as a pattern of holes in a stiff paper card. A press-down reader with spring-loaded pins completed electrical circuits wherever a hole allowed a pin to reach a cup of mercury below, and each completed circuit advanced an electromechanical counter dial. A sorting box with electrically triggered lids let clerks route cards into pockets by any punched characteristic, so the same deck could be recounted and cross-tabulated endlessly. It was not a computer, it neither calculated in a general sense nor stored programs, but it converted facts about the world into machine-readable form, and that conversion is the ancestral act of the information industry.

The 1890 census was the system's proving ground and triumph. Working with Hollerith's machines, the Census Office produced a rough national count, announced as 62,622,250 people, within months rather than years, and completed the full tabulation years faster than the previous census despite a larger population. Contemporary estimates credited the machines with saving the government roughly five million dollars and multiple years of labor. Hollerith, by then armed with a Columbia doctorate granted partly on the strength of the invention, commercialized it through the Tabulating Machine Company, incorporated in 1896. His business model proved as durable as his hardware: he leased the machines rather than selling them, retained ownership and servicing, and sold the punched cards, consumables that generated steady revenue with every use. Railroads, insurance companies, and foreign census bureaus in Russia, Austria, and elsewhere became customers.

The company's fortunes wobbled when the Census Bureau, resentful of Hollerith's pricing, backed a former employee named James Powers to build alternative machines for the 1910 count; Powers's firm would eventually fold into Remington Rand, IBM's future rival in both tabulators and computers. Squeezed out of his anchor customer, the aging and famously prickly Hollerith agreed in 1911 to sell his company into a merger arranged by the financier Charles Flint, receiving a substantial fortune and a consulting role. The merged entity, described in the next section, carried his cards, his leasing model, and his customer base forward into the century they would help define.

sections.heading: The 1911 Merger: Computing-Tabulating-Recording
sections.body:
The company that became IBM was assembled, not founded, and the assembler was Charles Ranlett Flint, a colorful New York financier known in the press as the father of trusts for his talent at rolling competing firms into consolidated companies. On June 16, 1911, Flint incorporated the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company, universally shortened to CTR, in New York State, merging four businesses: Hollerith's Tabulating Machine Company of Washington, D.C.; the International Time Recording Company of Endicott, New York, which made the clocks and card recorders with which factories tracked workers' hours; the Computing Scale Company of Dayton, Ohio, maker of shopkeepers' scales that computed price from weight; and the Bundy Manufacturing Company, an earlier time-clock maker already folded into the group. The logic was Flint's usual: reduce competition, diversify across products whose demand cycles differed, and float the combination on a generous valuation. CTR began life with roughly 1,300 employees, plants in Endicott, Dayton, Toronto, and Washington, and a grab-bag identity, scales, clocks, and census machines, that gave no hint of what it would become.

The early years were unglamorous and financially strained. The company carried heavy debt from the merger, and its parts operated as semi-independent fiefdoms under George W. Fairchild, a congressman and businessman who served as chairman. What changed everything was a hire. In 1914 Flint recruited Thomas J. Watson Sr., a forty-year-old sales executive who had risen to national sales manager of the National Cash Register Company under the domineering John H. Patterson, then been fired in one of Patterson's purges. Watson arrived under a cloud: he and other NCR executives had been convicted in 1913 of criminal antitrust violations for NCR's ruthless campaign against secondhand cash-register dealers. He refused a pardon that would have implied guilt; an appeals court ordered a retrial in 1915, and the government ultimately dropped the case. CTR's board made him general manager in 1914 and president in 1915 once the legal cloud thinned.

Watson bet the company's future on Hollerith's division. Scales and time clocks were respectable businesses, but tabulating machines were leased, generated recurring revenue, consumed proprietary punched cards by the millions, and served the accounting departments of the largest corporations and governments on earth, customers whose data needs only grew. He poured investment into the tabulating line, built a professional sales force on the NCR model, established quotas and commissions, and founded a research and development function in Endicott to keep the machines improving. Revenue roughly tripled across his first decade.

The name caught up with the ambition in stages. CTR's Canadian subsidiary had operated since 1917 as International Business Machines Company, Limited, a name Watson liked for its sweep. On February 14, 1924, the whole corporation was renamed International Business Machines Corporation, a grand title for a firm still selling meat scales, but Watson was naming the company he intended to build, not the one he had. Flint remained a director into the 1930s; Fairchild's son Sherman would later found Fairchild Camera, whose semiconductor division seeded Silicon Valley, one of history's tidy ironies. By the mid-1920s the pieces were in place: the cards, the leases, the sales culture, and the name.

sections.heading: Thomas J. Watson Sr. and the Making of IBM
sections.body:
Thomas John Watson Sr. ran IBM for four decades, from 1914 to 1956, and no large American corporation has ever borne one man's stamp more completely. Born in 1874 in upstate New York to a farming family, he began as a traveling salesman of sewing machines and pianos, then spent seventeen formative years at National Cash Register, where John Patterson had invented modern sales management: exclusive territories, quotas, canned sales pitches, conventions, and evangelical company spirit. Watson absorbed it all, softened Patterson's cruelty into paternalism, and rebuilt it at IBM as a total corporate culture that outsiders found somewhere between impressive and unsettling.

Its elements became famous. Salesmen wore dark suits, white shirts, and sober ties, projecting the respectability of bankers to the executives they called on. Alcohol was banned at company functions and discouraged everywhere. The slogan THINK, which Watson had coined at NCR in 1911, went up on walls in every office and factory, later giving its name to IBM's magazine and, decades on, to the ThinkPad. Star performers joined the Hundred Percent Club for making quota, celebrated at revival-style conventions at Endicott where employees sang from the official songbook, Songs of the IBM, first printed in 1931, whose anthem Ever Onward saluted Watson by name. The company built country clubs, paid for schooling, promoted from within, and, most consequentially, followed a practice of avoiding layoffs, which Watson maintained even through the Depression and which survived as an implicit lifetime-employment bargain until the crisis of the early 1990s. In exchange the company expected loyalty verging on devotion. Critics mocked the songs and the conformity; competitors envied the salesforce it produced.

Watson's strategic instincts compounded the culture. He understood earlier than almost anyone that data processing was a service relationship, not a hardware transaction: machines were leased, serviced by IBM engineers, and upgraded on IBM's schedule, while the punched cards, of which customers consumed carloads, were sold at handsome margins and, until the government intervened in 1936, were required to be IBM's own. Revenue therefore recurred, insulating the company from the sales cycles that whipsawed rivals. He invested relentlessly in engineering, hiring inventors like James Bryce, one of the era's most prolific patent holders, and funding the Endicott laboratory that turned out steadily faster tabulators, sorters, and the multiplying punches that crept toward true calculation. He was also an early and genuine internationalist, planting subsidiaries across Europe, Latin America, and Asia; by the 1930s the World Peace through World Trade motto expressed both conviction and market strategy, though his acceptance of a medal from Hitler's government in 1937, at the peak of IBM's German business, would stain his record permanently even after he returned it in 1940.

His compensation, tied by contract to a percentage of profits, made him for a time the highest-paid executive in America, celebrated in newspapers as the thousand-dollar-a-day man. He cultivated presidents, especially Franklin Roosevelt, and made IBM a fixture of world's fairs and civic causes. In May 1956, aged eighty-two, he formally handed the chief executive role to his son Thomas Watson Jr.; he died six weeks later, on June 19, 1956. He left a company of roughly 60,000 employees with revenues near 900 million dollars, utterly dominant in punched-card data processing, and, thanks to a succession he had resisted but not blocked, already turning toward the electronic computer he had never fully trusted.

sections.heading: The Punched-Card Business Between the Wars
sections.body:
Between the world wars, IBM perfected a technology that ran the paperwork of industrial civilization: the punched-card installation. Understanding it explains both IBM's wealth and the shape of the computer industry that followed. A customer, an insurance company, a railroad, a government bureau, rented a suite of interconnected machines. Keypunch operators, overwhelmingly women, transcribed source documents into holes in cards. Verifiers re-keyed the data to catch errors. Sorters arranged decks by any column at hundreds of cards per minute; collators merged and matched decks; and the accounting machine, or tabulator, read the decks and printed totals, subtotals, invoices, and reports. Wiring a removable plugboard customized each machine's behavior for a job, an ancestor of programming. Nothing in the room thought, but the ensemble mechanized bookkeeping on a scale hand clerks could never match, and once a company's records lived on IBM cards, switching suppliers meant re-punching its institutional memory, a lock-in competitors could rarely break.

The card itself became a strategic weapon in 1928, when IBM introduced the eighty-column card with slim rectangular holes, replacing the earlier forty-five-column round-hole format. The new card doubled capacity, was patented, and was incompatible with the machines of the archrival Remington Rand, which had absorbed James Powers's company; the format froze IBM's customers to IBM and survived into the 1970s as the universal symbol of computing, the size and shape, according to company lore, having originally been chosen to match the 1887 dollar bill so existing cash drawers could store cards. Card sales were an extraordinary business in themselves: by the mid-1930s IBM manufactured billions of cards a year in its own paper mills, and cards contributed a share of profits wildly out of proportion to their price, prompting the 1936 Supreme Court decision, discussed in the antitrust section, that struck down the requirement to buy cards from IBM.

The machines advanced steadily. The Type IV tabulator of the early 1920s added direct subtraction and printing. The Type 600 series multiplying punches, beginning in 1931, could multiply two numbers read from a card and punch the result, genuine arithmetic performed by relays, and scientific customers noticed: Columbia University's Wallace Eckert, with Watson's patronage, chained IBM machines together in the 1930s to compute astronomical tables, founding the Thomas J. Watson Astronomical Computing Bureau in 1937 and demonstrating that business machines could do science. The 405 Alphabetical Accounting Machine of 1934 handled letters as well as digits, opening payrolls and mailing lists fully to mechanization. Endicott's engineers, guided by James Bryce, filed patents at a pace that kept IBM's technical moat wide, and Watson's product philosophy, evolutionary improvement, ferocious service, and never stranding a customer's card files, kept the installed base growing through every economic weather.

By the end of the 1930s IBM held on the order of eighty to ninety percent of the American tabulating market, with Remington Rand a distant second, and its leased machines hummed in railroads, utilities, insurers, banks, factories, and every large agency of the federal government. The company Franklin Roosevelt's administrators reached for when the New Deal created sudden oceans of records, the subject of the next section, was already the indispensable infrastructure of organized information, a position it would translate, after 1950, into dominance of the computer age.

sections.heading: The Depression Gamble and Social Security
sections.body:
The Great Depression should have crushed a maker of expensive office machinery. Orders collapsed after 1929, and IBM's rivals cut production, laid off workers, and hunkered down. Watson did the opposite, and the resulting gamble, one of the most celebrated in American business history, defined IBM's trajectory for a generation. Convinced that demand would return and determined to protect both his skilled workforce and his no-layoff covenant, he kept the Endicott factories running through the early 1930s, building machines and parts for which no customers existed and warehousing the inventory. He expanded the sales school, raised research spending, and in 1932 committed roughly one million dollars, a serious sum for the company then, to a new engineering laboratory at Endicott, completed in 1933. The board grew restive as unsold tabulators piled up; Watson's position, by later accounts, was genuinely precarious. Two facts rescued it. First, the leasing model cushioned revenue: machines already installed kept paying rent even when new orders vanished, and card sales continued as long as customers processed anything at all. Second, the federal government was about to create the largest bookkeeping problem in the history of the world.

The Social Security Act, signed by President Roosevelt on August 14, 1935, required the government to track the wages of every covered worker in America, some twenty-six million people at the outset, continuously, for decades, so that benefits could be computed from lifetime earnings. Contemporaries called it the biggest accounting operation of all time, and it had to be running within months. When the new Social Security Board and the Treasury surveyed suppliers in 1936, only one company could deliver machines, cards, and trained support at the necessary scale immediately, because only one company had spent the Depression building inventory and training people for a demand that did not yet exist. IBM won the heart of the business, and its machines, including a collator developed with the application in mind, filled the government's vast processing center in Baltimore, where rows of punches, sorters, and tabulators maintained the earnings records of the nation. The New Deal's other creations, the Wagner Act's reporting requirements, the Agricultural Adjustment Administration, the WPA's payrolls, and new state unemployment systems, multiplied the demand. Government, previously one customer among many, became the anchor tenant of the information economy.

The numbers tell the story of the gamble's payoff. IBM's revenues, around nineteen million dollars in 1934, roughly doubled by the end of the decade, reaching about forty-six million dollars in 1940 while much of American industry was still clawing back to 1929 levels, and its workforce grew when most payrolls shrank. The episode also fixed the company's public identity: IBM was now the firm that ran the paperwork of the modern administrative state, trusted with the records on which citizens' pensions depended. Watson's closeness to Roosevelt, whom he supported publicly and advised informally, reinforced the relationship, and wags said the initials stood for International Business Machines abroad and Internal Business Machines in Washington.

Inside the company, the Depression years hardened the lessons Watson preached: invest through the trough, protect the workforce, trust recurring revenue, and be ready when demand arrives, principles his successors would invoke at every subsequent crisis. The same years also deepened the habits, supreme self-confidence and a sense of indispensability, that antitrust enforcers and, much later, nimbler competitors would eventually punish. Both inheritances traveled together into the war that came next.

sections.heading: IBM in World War II
sections.body:
The Second World War industrialized information, and IBM stood at the center of it, in ways the company celebrated and in one way it has spent decades answering for. In the United States, Watson placed the company at the government's service after Pearl Harbor, capping profit on war production at one and a half percent and directing even that into a fund for the widows and orphans of IBM war dead. The Endicott and new Poughkeepsie works turned out munitions and materiel, more than three million dollars' worth a month at peak, including M1 carbines and Browning Automatic Rifles, bombsight components, and fire-control gear. The core business mattered more: punched-card installations multiplied through every service and agency, running draft records, payrolls, logistics, aircraft production schedules, rationing, and casualty accounting. Mobile Machine Records Units carried IBM equipment close behind the front lines, tabulating unit strength and supply; by war's end the Army alone operated hundreds of such units. Cryptanalysis leaned on the machines as well: the Navy's OP-20-G and the Army's Arlington Hall used rooms full of modified IBM tabulating equipment to sift enemy message traffic for patterns, an unglamorous complement to the electromechanical bombes and a direct rehearsal for computing.

The war also produced IBM's first true computer-adjacent machine. The Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator, conceived by Harvard's Howard Aiken and built by IBM at Endicott between 1939 and 1943, was an electromechanical monster fifty-one feet long, with three-quarters of a million parts, capable of executing long sequences of arithmetic from punched paper tape. Presented to Harvard in 1944, where it became famous as the Harvard Mark I, it computed ballistics tables and ran calculations for the Manhattan Project, including work John von Neumann brought for the implosion design. The dedication ended in a legendary rupture: Aiken's press release slighted IBM's engineers, and Watson, who had paid for the machine, arrived in Cambridge incandescent. The feud pushed IBM to build its own showcase, the Selective Sequence Electronic Calculator of 1948, displayed behind glass at the Manhattan headquarters, and stung the company toward electronics.

The dark chapter concerns Germany. IBM's German subsidiary, Deutsche Hollerith Maschinen Gesellschaft, or Dehomag, was the company's most successful foreign operation, and its machines served the Nazi state after 1933, including in the censuses of 1933 and 1939 that registered the population by ancestry, and in railroad administration and concentration-camp record offices, where the Hollerith department was a fixture. Edwin Black's 2001 book IBM and the Holocaust assembled documents arguing that the New York parent, and Watson personally, maintained profitable oversight of this business longer and more knowingly than the company ever acknowledged, managing it through European subsidiaries even after 1941. IBM has responded that it lost effective control of Dehomag under the Nazi regime, that the relevant records were largely destroyed or seized, and that historians it engaged found no evidence the parent directed wartime operations. Scholars continue to dispute the degree of knowledge and control; what is not disputed is that Hollerith technology, much of it IBM-originated, served the machinery of persecution, and that Watson's 1937 medal from Hitler's government, returned in 1940, symbolized a relationship pursued too long. The episode stands as the permanent caution attached to the company's wartime story: the same neutrality of infrastructure that let IBM's machines run Social Security let their German cousins run something unspeakable.

sections.heading: Into Electronics: the 701, the 650, and the 1401
sections.body:
Electronics entered IBM over the founder's hesitation and through his son's conviction. Thomas Watson Jr., back from the war a decorated bomber pilot, saw in vacuum-tube calculation the future his father's relay machines could not reach, and the trigger was competitive: Remington Rand's UNIVAC I, delivered to the Census Bureau in 1951 and famous overnight for calling the 1952 election on CBS, threatened to make IBM look like the past. The company's first answer, begun as a Korean War project and initially called the Defense Calculator, was announced in 1952 as the IBM 701, a vacuum-tube, stored-program scientific computer using Williams-tube memory and magnetic tape. Only nineteen were built, leased at roughly fifteen thousand dollars a month to aircraft companies, laboratories, and the government, but the 701 announced that IBM was in the computer business, and the 702 and the 700-series successors carried its architecture into commercial work.

The machine that actually created the computer market, however, was modest by design. The IBM 650 Magnetic Drum Data Processing Machine, announced in 1953 and first delivered in December 1954, stored data on a spinning magnetic drum, rented for around three thousand dollars a month, and was engineered to slot into existing punched-card installations rather than replace them. IBM projected modest sales; customers ordered it by the hundreds, and by the end of production in 1962 nearly two thousand had been built, making the 650 the first mass-produced computer in the world, the Model T of computing in the standard phrase. A shrewd education program magnified its influence: IBM offered universities discounts approaching sixty percent, seeding campuses across America with 650s, and a generation of programmers, including Donald Knuth, who dedicated his Art of Computer Programming to the 650, learned the craft on its drum. Meanwhile the SAGE air-defense project, in which IBM built the enormous duplexed AN/FSQ-7 computers for MIT's Lincoln Laboratory from the mid-1950s, fifty-six machines for over twenty control centers, paid the company roughly half a billion dollars and, more valuably, taught it mass production of magnetic-core memory, real-time processing, printed circuits, and networked operation, capabilities that flowed straight into commercial products.

The transistorized 1401, announced in October 1959, completed the conquest. Aimed at ordinary accounting departments, it rented from about twenty-five hundred dollars a month, ran punched-card jobs faster than any tabulator, and came paired with the 1403 chain printer, whose 600-line-per-minute output was so far ahead of the field that some customers bought the computer to get the printer. IBM expected perhaps a thousand orders; within weeks it had several times that, and by the mid-1960s more than ten thousand 1401s were installed, roughly half the computers on earth. The 1400 and 700/7000 series together carried IBM to about seventy percent of the exploding computer market by the early 1960s, with the remainder split among the seven dwarfs, as the press called GE, RCA, Burroughs, UNIVAC, NCR, Control Data, and Honeywell.

Watson Jr., president from 1952 and chief executive from 1956, had bet on hiring electrical engineers by the thousand and won. But success bred a new problem: by 1960 IBM was selling a half-dozen incompatible computer families, each with its own peripherals and software, each straining engineering resources, and customers who outgrew one machine faced rewriting everything to move to the next. The company's answer to that self-inflicted chaos became the biggest business gamble of the century, and the next section's subject.

sections.heading: The System/360 Gamble
sections.body:
By 1961 IBM's computer lines formed an archipelago: the 1401 for small commercial shops, the 7070 and 7080 for larger ones, the 7090 for science, and others, none compatible with any other. Every line needed its own peripherals, its own software, its own engineers, and customers who grew had to convert their programs by hand, an agony that made them shop competitors at exactly the moment IBM should have owned them. An internal task force, the SPREAD committee, delivered its report in December 1961 with a radical recommendation: scrap everything and build a single unified family of computers, spanning the whole market from small to enormous, all executing the same instruction set, all sharing the same peripherals, so that a customer could start small and grow without ever rewriting software. Compatibility across a performance range of roughly twenty-five to one had never been attempted; it would be achieved through microprogramming, with smaller models emulating the common architecture in microcode, a technique adapted from Maurice Wilkes's ideas by the engineers under chief architect Gene Amdahl, with Fred Brooks managing the architecture and Bob Evans the program.

Thomas Watson Jr. approved what the company came to call a bet-the-business decision. The development budget ran to some five billion dollars over four years, about three-quarters of a billion for engineering and the rest for factories, including IBM's move to manufacture its own hybrid microelectronics, at a time when the company's annual revenue was near three billion; Fortune's famous 1966 account ran under the title IBM's $5,000,000,000 Gamble. The risk was doubled by self-cannibalization: announcing the new family would freeze sales of every existing line, and any slip would leave the company with nothing to sell. On April 7, 1964, from Poughkeepsie and 165 cities simultaneously, IBM announced System/360, named for the full circle of applications it meant to serve: six processor models spanning a performance range later extended further, over forty peripherals including new disk and tape units, and a promise of upward and downward compatibility that the industry had never heard before. The announcement also standardized the eight-bit byte, the 360's architecture fixing conventions, byte addressing, the EBCDIC character set, hexadecimal notation in practice, that shaped all subsequent computing.

The gamble nearly failed in the execution. Orders overwhelmed the plan, exceeding a thousand in the first month and forcing IBM to quintuple production capacity; component shortages and quality crises followed, and the software was worse. OS/360, the flagship operating system, fell years behind, consumed thousands of programmer-years, and taught its manager Fred Brooks the lessons he distilled in The Mythical Man-Month in 1975, including Brooks's law, that adding manpower to a late software project makes it later. Watson later wrote that the program brought IBM closer to disaster than anything in its history. But the machines shipped, from 1965 in volume, and the market's verdict was overwhelming: within two years the 360 line had reset the industry, competitors were forced either to clone it, as RCA tried, or flee to niches, and IBM's revenues more than doubled between 1964 and 1970, with its market share holding near seventy percent.

The strategic masterstroke was the architecture itself as an institution. The System/370 of 1970 extended it with virtual memory; successive generations, 303x, 308x, 3090, System/390, and the zSeries from 2000, preserved compatibility, so that programs written for a 1964 System/360 can still run on the z-series mainframes IBM sells today, six decades of continuity unmatched anywhere in technology. The 360 also fixed the industry's economics: with hardware unified, software and peripherals became the battlegrounds, and IBM's dominance of the whole stack drew the antitrust siege described next, while the plug-compatible industry, led by Amdahl himself after he left in 1970, grew up inside the standard IBM had created.

sections.heading: Inventions That Built Modern Computing
sections.body:
For half a century IBM's laboratories produced a disproportionate share of computing's foundational technology, and a tour of the highlights doubles as a history of the field. Magnetic disk storage was born in San Jose in 1956, when a team under Reynold Johnson shipped the RAMAC 305, whose disk unit stacked fifty aluminum platters, each twenty-four inches across, spinning at 1,200 rpm under a moving read-write head. It stored five megabytes, about the text of a long novel, leased for roughly 3,200 dollars a month, and replaced rooms of card files with random access, the R and A of its name. Every hard drive since is its descendant, and IBM kept advancing the line: the removable disk pack of the early 1960s, the sealed low-mass-head Winchester technology of the 3340 in 1973 that defined drive design for decades, the first giant-magnetoresistive heads in the 1990s, before selling the disk business to Hitachi in 2002.

Programming languages owe IBM their commercial birth. In 1957 a team under John Backus delivered FORTRAN for the 704, the first widely used high-level language, whose optimizing compiler proved that programs written in formulas could run nearly as fast as hand-coded assembly; science and engineering still run on its descendants. Backus later co-authored the Backus-Naur Form for describing language grammar and won the 1977 Turing Award. In 1970 the IBM researcher Edgar F. Codd published A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks, recasting databases as mathematical relations queryable without knowledge of storage layout; the System R prototype at San Jose validated the idea and produced SQL, written by Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce. In a celebrated irony, IBM, protective of its hierarchical IMS product, moved slowly, and the first commercial relational database came from the tiny company that became Oracle in 1979; Codd received the 1981 Turing Award, and relational systems, IBM's DB2 among them, came to hold most of the world's structured data. John Cocke's 801 project in the mid-1970s distilled the RISC idea, that simpler instruction sets enable faster machines, earning Cocke the 1987 Turing Award and seeding IBM's POWER architecture and, by influence, nearly every modern processor. Fran Allen's compiler-optimization work made her, in 2006, the first woman to win the Turing Award.

The component inventions are just as pervasive. Robert Dennard invented the one-transistor dynamic RAM cell at Yorktown Heights in 1966, patented in 1968; every stick of memory in every device on earth uses it, and Dennard scaling named the physics that drove miniaturization for forty years. An IBM team under Alan Shugart introduced the eight-inch floppy disk in 1971, originally to load microcode into System/370 machines. George Laurer of IBM designed the Universal Product Code barcode adopted by the grocery industry in 1973, building on the 1949 patent of Norman Woodland, himself an IBM employee for decades, and a pack of Wrigley's gum scanned in an Ohio supermarket in 1974 opened the barcode era. IBM Zurich physicists Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer built the scanning tunneling microscope in 1981, imaging individual atoms and winning the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physics; their colleagues Georg Bednorz and Alex Müller discovered high-temperature superconductivity in copper oxides in 1986 and won the Nobel the following year, back-to-back prizes from one laboratory. Earlier, Leo Esaki, who joined IBM Research in 1960, shared the 1973 Nobel for electron tunneling. Add Benoit Mandelbrot's fractal geometry, developed on IBM computers at Yorktown, the excimer-laser surgery patents behind LASIK, copper interconnects and silicon-on-insulator chipmaking in the 1990s, and the pattern is clear: for decades, when computing needed a new physical or mathematical foundation, the odds were good it came from IBM Research.

sections.heading: Antitrust: Consent Decrees, the 1969 Case, and Unbundling
sections.body:
IBM spent more of the twentieth century under antitrust scrutiny than any technology company in history, and the government's shadow shaped its conduct as much as any competitor did. The first blow landed in 1936, when the Supreme Court, in IBM v. United States, upheld an order forbidding IBM from requiring lessees of its machines to buy IBM punched cards, a tying arrangement that had made cards a fountain of monopoly profit. The second came in 1952, when the Justice Department sued over the tabulating business wholesale; the case ended in the consent decree of January 1956, under which IBM agreed to sell machines as well as lease them, on non-discriminatory terms, to license patents for reasonable royalties, and to run its service bureau at arm's length. The decree's timing was providential for the industry: it took effect just as computing began, and its sale-versus-lease and licensing provisions enabled the leasing companies, plug-compatible manufacturers, and service firms that would populate the computer economy.

The centerpiece arrived on January 17, 1969, the last business day of the Johnson administration, when the Department of Justice filed United States v. IBM, alleging monopolization of the general-purpose digital computer market, IBM's share then being on the order of seventy percent, and seeking nothing less than the company's breakup. The government pointed to practices including bundling hardware, software, and services in a single price, announcing future products early to freeze competitors' sales, and fighting the plug-compatible peripheral makers with targeted pricing. The litigation became a byword for judicial gigantism: discovery produced tens of millions of pages, the trial began in 1975 and ran six years before Judge David Edelstein, seven hundred witnesses gave testimony live or by deposition, and the transcript passed one hundred thousand pages. IBM's defense, marshaled by armies of lawyers under general counsel and future Attorney General Nicholas Katzenbach, contested every inch. On January 8, 1982, the same day the government settled its case against AT&T by dismembering the Bell System, Assistant Attorney General William Baxter dismissed the IBM suit as without merit, ending thirteen years of litigation with no formal remedy.

Calling the case remedy-free, however, misreads its effects. Facing the suit's imminent filing, IBM announced in June 1969 that it would unbundle: henceforth software, education, and systems-engineering services would be priced and sold separately from hardware. Unbundling, implemented from 1970, is widely credited as the founding charter of the independent software products industry, since programs now competed on price against IBM's own rather than arriving free inside the machine rental. For the following decade the company priced, announced, and designed with one eye on the courtroom, and veterans of the era described a culture of lawyers vetting slide decks; some historians argue this litigation caution helps explain IBM's restraint in the 1970s and its arm's-length handling of the PC suppliers described later. The European Commission pressed a parallel case over interface information in the early 1980s, settled in 1984 with disclosure undertakings that lasted a decade.

The 1956 decree itself outlived its world: its last provisions were finally phased out by court order around the turn of the millennium, decades after tabulators vanished. The full antitrust arc, from cards to computers, stands as the classic study in how competition law and a dominant platform company shape each other, cited in every subsequent technology monopoly fight from AT&T to Microsoft to the present.

sections.heading: The IBM PC and the Clone Wars
sections.body:
At the end of the 1970s the microcomputer boom, Apple II, Tandy, Commodore, was happening entirely without IBM, whose committees took years to approve products and whose customers were data-processing departments, not hobbyists. In 1980 corporate management gave William Lowe's Boca Raton, Florida, unit a mandate unprecedented in company history: build a personal computer in one year, free of the usual process. The team of about a dozen, soon led by Don Estridge under the codename Project Chess, met the deadline by violating every IBM tradition at once. The machine used outside components, an Intel 8088 processor, off-the-shelf chips, and outside software; it had an open, documented expansion bus, with schematics and BIOS listings published in a technical reference manual so third parties could build cards and programs; and it would be sold through retail stores like ComputerLand and Sears, not leased by systems engineers. For the operating system IBM went to Microsoft, a Seattle company known for language products, after contact with Digital Research over CP/M famously miscarried; Microsoft bought a working system called 86-DOS from Seattle Computer Products for a sum reported around 75,000 dollars, polished it into PC DOS, and, in the deal's history-bending clause, retained the right to license its own version, MS-DOS, to other manufacturers.

The IBM Personal Computer, model 5150, was announced on August 12, 1981, at 1,565 dollars for a base configuration with 16 kilobytes of memory and a cassette interface. IBM's name did what no startup's could: it certified the microcomputer as serious business equipment overnight. The company had projected some 240,000 units over five years; it shipped on that order within a couple of years and by the mid-1980s had sold millions more, while Lotus 1-2-3, the spreadsheet built for the PC in 1983, became the application that justified the purchase. Estridge's unit, run as an independent business inside the corporation, grew into a division that by itself would have ranked among America's largest computer companies; Estridge himself died in the Delta Flight 191 crash in 1985, mourned as the father of the PC.

Openness, the decision that made the platform, also unmade IBM's control of it. The only proprietary component was the BIOS firmware, and in 1982-83 Compaq famously clean-room reverse-engineered it, lawyers attesting that the engineers who wrote the new code had never seen IBM's, and shipped a compatible portable that earned 111 million dollars in its first year, the fastest start in business history to that point. Phoenix Technologies then sold clean-room BIOS to all comers from 1984, and the clone industry was born: Compaq, Dell, and dozens of Asian manufacturers sold IBM compatibility without IBM margins, while Intel and Microsoft, whose chips and operating system every clone bought, collected rent on the entire standard. IBM's counterattacks failed sequentially. The 1984 PCjr home computer flopped over its chiclet keyboard and price. The 1987 PS/2 line introduced the proprietary Micro Channel bus to re-close the architecture; the market bought the PS/2's other contributions, VGA graphics and the 3.5-inch floppy, and refused the bus, as the clone camp standardized around alternatives. OS/2, the advanced operating system IBM and Microsoft began jointly in 1985 and shipped in 1987, was orphaned when Windows 3.0's 1990 success led Microsoft to abandon the partnership; the divorce of 1990-91 left Microsoft holding the industry's future.

By the early 1990s IBM was one clone maker among many on a standard it had created, profitable share leader some years, loss-maker others. The PC had multiplied the industry a hundredfold and centered it on two suppliers, neither of them IBM, a strategic outcome business schools have dissected ever since, and a principal tributary of the corporate crisis described next.

sections.heading: The Early-1990s Crisis
sections.body:
Around 1990 IBM stood at what looked like a summit: revenues near sixty-nine billion dollars, six billion in profit, four hundred thousand employees, and the most admired name in business. Within three years it was in the deepest crisis of its history, reporting the largest losses American business had ever seen and openly discussing its own dismemberment. The causes had been accumulating for a decade. The mainframe, still contributing the bulk of profits through hardware margins reported to approach sixty percent, was being flanked from below: microprocessors improved on the curve Gordon Moore had described, and networks of cheap PCs and Unix servers from Sun, HP, and Digital began doing work that had required a glass-house System/370, a shift the industry called client-server and downsizing. IBM knew, its own people had invented much of the technology, but the company's economics, culture, and sales incentives all defended the mainframe, and its famous contention system of consensus management had curdled into paralysis: proposals died in committees, and insiders joked that products shipped despite the process. Meanwhile the PC business it had created was ceding profit to Intel, Microsoft, Compaq, and Dell, and IBM's costs, built for perpetual growth, no longer fit its revenues.

The financial unraveling was swift. Profits fell in 1990; in 1991 IBM lost 2.8 billion dollars, its first loss ever; 1992 brought a five billion dollar loss, and 1993 an 8.1 billion dollar loss, then the largest single-year corporate loss in American history, the three years together totaling nearly sixteen billion, much of it restructuring charges as the company shrank. Employment, 407,000 at the 1986 peak, fell toward 300,000 by 1992 and near 220,000 by 1994; in 1993 the company formally abandoned the no-layoff practice that had defined it since Watson Sr., a cultural rupture employees experienced as the breaking of a covenant. The stock collapsed from a 1987 high above 43 dollars, split-adjusted, to under 11 by mid-1993, wiping out some seventy billion in market value, and in January 1993 the board halved the dividend, unthinkable a few years before.

Chairman John Akers, a career IBMer running the company since 1985, responded with successive restructurings, early-retirement waves, and finally, in late 1991, a plan to split IBM into more than a dozen autonomous units, thirteen Baby Blues in the press's phrase, printers, storage, semiconductors, PCs, services, each to compete independently and perhaps be sold to the public, on the theory that the integrated company was worth less than its parts. The printer business was actually spun off, becoming Lexmark in 1991. But losses deepened, the breakup logic frightened big customers who depended on IBM's integration, and confidence in management evaporated. On January 26, 1993, Akers resigned under board pressure, and a search committee led by directors Jim Burke and Tom Murphy conducted the most public CEO hunt in memory, famously being turned down by or passing over the era's celebrity executives, Jack Welch, Larry Bossidy, Bill Gates was even asked his opinion, before settling on a candidate from entirely outside the industry.

Commentators wrote the company's obituary in earnest; The Economist and respected authors declared the mainframe dead and IBM a dinosaur unable to survive the ecosystem it had created. The stage was set for one of the most studied corporate turnarounds ever, the subject of the next section.

sections.heading: Lou Gerstner and the Services Turnaround
sections.body:
Louis V. Gerstner Jr. took over as IBM's chairman and chief executive on April 1, 1993, the first outsider ever to run the company: a McKinsey partner turned American Express president turned chief executive of RJR Nabisco, a manager of businesses rather than a technologist, which was precisely the board's point. His first decisions reversed the prevailing plan. Within months he stopped the breakup, concluding after listening to the big customers that IBM's unique asset was exactly its integration, the ability to deliver and stitch together all the pieces of computing for enterprises drowning in incompatible technology. At an early press conference he uttered the most quoted line of the era, that the last thing IBM needs right now is a vision, meaning that execution, cash, and customers came first. The immediate surgery was brutal: a further restructuring charge of 8.9 billion dollars in mid-1993, tens of thousands more job cuts on top of Akers's, sales of assets including much of the art collection and the Federal Systems division, sold to Loral in 1994, and a mainframe pricing reset that traded margin for volume while engineering moved the line to cheaper CMOS microprocessors, a transition completed through the 1990s that saved the franchise. The company returned to profit in 1994, three billion dollars, its first profitable year since 1990.

The strategic rebuild had three pillars. First, services. Under Dennie Welsh and then Sam Palmisano, IBM Global Services grew from an outsourcing sideline into the world's largest information-technology services organization, running customers' data centers, integrating their systems whoever made them, and by 2001 employing roughly 150,000 people and billing near thirty-five billion dollars, passing hardware to become the company's largest business. Services changed the company's center of gravity from products to relationships, exactly the integration argument that had justified keeping IBM whole. Second, software as a discipline. Gerstner consolidated scattered software efforts into a brand-led group, bought Lotus Development in 1995 for 3.5 billion dollars in what was then the largest software acquisition ever, a rare hostile takeover executed gently, and Tivoli Systems in 1996, and repositioned IBM's middleware, WebSphere, MQ, DB2, to run on everyone's hardware, not just IBM's. Third, the network bet. From 1995 Gerstner reoriented marketing and development around the internet under the banner e-business, a term IBM's advertising coined and made ubiquitous, selling the picture of the web as the next platform for transactions and IBM as the company that would wire commerce to it, a framing that let a ninety-year-old firm claim the future credibly. In 1999-2000 IBM startled the industry again by embracing Linux, committing a publicized billion dollars in 2001, porting it across its hardware, and defending it legally, open source as a weapon against proprietary rivals.

Culture was, by Gerstner's own account, the hardest part, the thing he later said culture was not just one aspect of the game but the game itself. He dismantled the contention bureaucracy, tied pay to company rather than unit results, replaced the dress code with customer common sense, and forced outward focus with programs like Operation Bear Hug, executives dispatched to listen to customers. The results compounded: by 2001 revenues were about eighty-six billion dollars, earnings near eight billion, and the stock had risen roughly eightfold from the 1993 trough.
