Gerstner handed the chief executive role to Sam Palmisano in March 2002 and told the story himself in Who Says Elephants Can't Dance?, the memoir whose title became shorthand for the whole episode: the canonical proof that a giant, given ruthless honesty about its situation, can turn.

sections.heading: Deep Blue, Watson, and the 2000s Reinvention
sections.body:
Two exhibition matches bracketed IBM's turn of the millennium and did more for its public identity than any product campaign. The first was chess. Deep Blue, a project that had entered IBM Research with Carnegie Mellon graduate students Feng-hsiung Hsu and Murray Campbell, paired massively parallel search with custom chess chips, evaluating on the order of two hundred million positions per second. In February 1996 in Philadelphia it lost a match to world champion Garry Kasparov three and a half to two and a half, but took the first game, the first time a computer had beaten a reigning champion at classical time controls. The May 1997 rematch in New York, upgraded machine, ended with Deep Blue winning three and a half to two and a half, sealed by a crushing final game; Kasparov, shaken, accused the team of human interference he never substantiated, and the moment entered history as the symbolic passing of a human intellectual bastion. IBM retired the machine immediately, banking the demonstration that it could marshal research into spectacle.

The business, meanwhile, was being remade under Sam Palmisano, chief executive from 2002, around a thesis he had helped build in Global Services: profits were migrating from hardware to services and software, so IBM would climb the value chain and shed commodity businesses without sentiment. In 2002 the company bought PricewaterhouseCoopers Consulting for about 3.5 billion dollars, adding thirty thousand consultants and making IBM the largest business-consulting force in the world. Then it began the sheddings that would have been heresy a generation earlier: hard drives to Hitachi in 2002; and in December 2004 the announcement that stunned the industry, the sale of the entire Personal Computer division, ThinkPad included, to China's Lenovo for roughly 1.75 billion dollars, completed in May 2005. The company that had legitimized the PC exited it, arguing the margins now lived elsewhere, and continued the logic later by selling the x86 server line to Lenovo in 2014 and spinning off chip manufacturing to GlobalFoundries the same year. Palmisano's globally integrated enterprise doctrine moved delivery to global centers, with Indian headcount growing past American, and his commitment to shareholder returns, codified in public earnings-per-share roadmaps, delivered buybacks and steady EPS growth that critics would later argue starved investment.

The second exhibition came in February 2011, when Watson, a question-answering system built by David Ferrucci's team on the DeepQA architecture, running on POWER7 servers and trained on encyclopedic text, defeated Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter, the two greatest champions of the quiz show Jeopardy!, in a nationally televised two-game match, finishing with 77,147 dollars to their 24,000 and 21,600; Jennings annotated his final answer with welcome to our new computer overlords. Watson was a genuine research landmark in open-domain question answering and a marketing triumph, and IBM, under Virginia Rometty, chief executive from January 2012, built a business unit and a headquarters around it, aiming above all at medicine. The sequel disappointed: Watson Health's ambitions to revolutionize oncology collided with messy clinical data and overpromising, flagship partnerships such as MD Anderson's ended, and IBM sold Watson Health's data assets to a private-equity firm in 2022, a case study now taught about the gap between demonstration and deployment. Rometty's tenure wrestled the harder structural problem, that cloud computing's rise favored Amazon, Microsoft, and Google while IBM's revenue declined for over twenty consecutive quarters, and her answer, examined next, was the largest acquisition in the company's history.

sections.heading: Red Hat, Kyndryl, and IBM Research's Long Legacy
sections.body:
IBM's latest reinvention was purchased in one stroke. On October 28, 2018, Virginia Rometty announced that IBM would acquire Red Hat, the Raleigh-based leader of enterprise open source, whose Linux distribution and OpenShift container platform ran across every cloud, for 190 dollars a share, about thirty-four billion dollars, by far the largest deal in IBM history and one of the largest software acquisitions ever. The close, in July 2019, committed IBM to the strategy its architect, Red Hat champion and cloud chief Arvind Krishna, called hybrid cloud: conceding that enterprises would spread work across Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and their own data centers, and selling the neutral software layer, Linux and Kubernetes-based, that lets them move it. Krishna became chief executive in April 2020, and completed the focusing move in November 2021 by spinning off the managed-infrastructure half of Global Services, the data-center-running business of the Gerstner era, as an independent public company, Kyndryl, with about ninety thousand employees, leaving a smaller IBM built around hybrid cloud, software, consulting, mainframes, and, in its latest branding, artificial intelligence through the watsonx platform launched in 2023. The company that once did everything now deliberately does less: revenue around sixty-two billion dollars in 2023, roughly 280,000 employees, but margins and focus its recent predecessors lacked, with the z-series mainframe, still binary-compatible with 1964, quietly processing the bulk of the world's credit-card transactions by the company's oft-cited claim.

Any final accounting of IBM rests on its research institution, formalized in 1945 with the Watson Scientific Computing Laboratory at Columbia University and headquartered from 1961 at the Eero Saarinen-designed Thomas J. Watson Research Center in Yorktown Heights, New York, with sister laboratories in Zurich, Almaden, Haifa, Tokyo, Delhi, Nairobi, and beyond. Its trophy case is unique in industry: six Nobel laureates, Leo Esaki in 1973 for tunneling, Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer in 1986 for the scanning tunneling microscope, Georg Bednorz and Alex Müller in 1987 for high-temperature superconductivity; six Turing Award winners, including Backus, Codd, Cocke, and Fran Allen; and a patent operation that led the United States in grants for twenty-nine consecutive years, from 1993 through 2021, before the company deliberately stepped off that treadmill. Beyond the inventions cataloged earlier, the laboratories produced Ted Codd's relational theory, the Data Encryption Standard's Lucifer cipher in the 1970s, copper interconnects in 1997, silicon-on-insulator and strained silicon, the Blue Gene supercomputers that led the world's rankings in the 2000s, and Benoit Mandelbrot's fractal geometry.

The current research banner is quantum computing, where IBM has led the superconducting-qubit approach in public: the first cloud-accessible quantum processor in 2016, the 127-qubit Eagle chip in 2021, the 433-qubit Osprey in 2022, and the 1,121-qubit Condor in 2023, alongside the modular Quantum System Two and a roadmap aimed at error-corrected machines; whether quantum advantage arrives on IBM's schedule or anyone's, the company has made itself the field's most visible industrial laboratory. Looking back down the whole arc, census tabulators to punched-card empire, mainframe hegemony to PC self-disruption, near-death to services rebirth, and now hybrid cloud and qubits, the through-line is not any technology but an institutional habit: roughly once a generation, IBM has torn up its own dominant business and rebuilt around the next one, sometimes late, sometimes brutally, so far always in time. That habit, more than THINK signs or any single machine, is the history of IBM.
